text: With the Service Desk workstream scoped, the next step is talking to the people who will actually use it. This lesson simulates structured interviews with each hospital system's current help-desk lead, and shows how their answers turn into one written requirements document.

Each interview surfaces something real and specific, not a generic wish list. St. Catherine's lead runs the most mature process of the three and worries about losing precision — their detailed, multi-tier categories feed real reporting and staffing decisions today, and they need that level of detail preserved on the new platform, not simplified away. Lakeshore's lead worries less about the data fields themselves and more about control — who actually gets to change their categories once a corporate-level platform launches, and whether that decision can be made without them. And Prairie View's lead, after a forced consolidation eight years ago that cost two senior IT leaders their jobs, cares most about a visible say in the rollout and training plan itself — proof, in practice, that this time is genuinely different.

Lay all three side by side and a real conflict appears immediately. St. Catherine's files a ticket three levels deep, under hardware, laptop, docking station. Lakeshore uses a flat category list built for how their own team actually works. Prairie View's process is informal enough that most tickets are just free text. These three approaches do not map onto each other cleanly, and that's not something you solve by interviewing more carefully — it's a genuine structural conflict between three legitimate ways of working.

A real requirements document organizes all of this into four sections a reviewer can actually act on: functional requirements, what each system's agents must actually be able to do day one; non-functional requirements, like domain-scoped visibility, reporting access, and the performance each system expects; stakeholder sign-off, confirming each system's section was reviewed and is accurate; and an open-conflicts section that states the categorization mismatch plainly, names the systems affected, and flags it for a deliberate scoping decision — rather than quietly resolving it in whoever's favor seems easiest to configure.
That open conflict is exactly what Lesson 14 has to resolve — deciding, deliberately and in writing, what Phase 1 actually includes.
